translations.title: Multiples of a Number PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Multiples of a Number PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Factors and Multiples”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.OA.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1–100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1–100 is prime or composite. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Multiples of a Number PLC Activity. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 6 equal groups with 7 objects in each group. The product is 6 × 7 = 42; therefore 42 ÷ 6 = 7. Example 2: Arrange 8 equal groups with 2 objects in each group. The product is 8 × 2 = 16; therefore 16 ÷ 8 = 2.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 6 groups and 7 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 6 by 7 to get 42. Step 3: interpret 42 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 42 ÷ 6 = 7. Step 1: identify 8 groups and 2 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 8 by 2 to get 16. Step 3: interpret 16 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 16 ÷ 8 = 2.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Multiples of a Number PLC Activity. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Multiples of a Number PLC Activity. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń rozumuje o równych grupach, tablicach, czynnikach, iloczynach, ilorazach i nieznanej wielkości grupy. Mnożenie i dzielenie są działaniami wzajemnie odwrotnymi. translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Ułóż 7 równych grup po 2 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 7 × 2 = 14, więc 14 ÷ 7 = 2. Przykład 2: Ułóż 7 równych grup po 5 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 7 × 5 = 35, więc 35 ÷ 7 = 5.

translations.title: Find Factors and Multiples
translations.explanation: Find Factors and Multiples is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Factors and Multiples”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.OA.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1–100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1–100 is prime or composite. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Find Factors and Multiples. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 6 equal groups with 6 objects in each group. The product is 6 × 6 = 36; therefore 36 ÷ 6 = 6. Example 2: Arrange 6 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 6 × 3 = 18; therefore 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 6 groups and 6 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 6 by 6 to get 36. Step 3: interpret 36 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 36 ÷ 6 = 6. Step 1: identify 6 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 6 by 3 to get 18. Step 3: interpret 18 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Find Factors and Multiples. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Find Factors and Multiples. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

translations.title: Same Size, Related Sizes PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Same Size, Related Sizes PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Fraction Equivalence and Comparison”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.NF.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n × a)/(n × b) by using visual fraction models, with a ttention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions. Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Same Size, Related Sizes PLC Activity. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/6 + 4/6 = 6/6. This equals 1/1 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8. This equals 5/4 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 6ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+4=6. Step 3: keep denominator 6. Step 4: simplify 6/6 to 1/1 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 8ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 4+6=10. Step 3: keep denominator 8. Step 4: simplify 10/8 to 5/4 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Same Size, Related Sizes PLC Activity. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Same Size, Related Sizes PLC Activity. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — Same Size, Related Sizes PLC Activity. Mianownik mówi, na ile równych części podzielono całość, a licznik wskazuje liczbę takich części. Ułamki równoważne opisują tę samą liczbę. Przy dodawaniu i odejmowaniu części muszą mieć ten sam rozmiar; przy mnożeniu i dzieleniu trzeba interpretować skalowanie lub podział.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 2/6 + 4/6 = 6/6. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 1/1. Przykład 2: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 5/4.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/6, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 2+4=6. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 6. Krok 4: skróć 6/6 do 1/1 i porównaj wynik z 1. Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/8, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 4+6=10. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 8. Krok 4: skróć 10/8 do 5/4 i porównaj wynik z 1.

translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — Same Size, Related Sizes PLC Activity. Rozpoznaj jednostkę ułamkową, zachowaj równe części, w razie potrzeby użyj ułamków równoważnych, wykonaj działanie i sprawdź wielkość wyniku.

For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.) c. translations.title: Lots of Fractions to Add

The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number. a. Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b. For example, use a visual fraction model to represent 5/4 as the product 5 × (1/4), recording the conclusion by the equation 5/4 = 5 × (1/4). b. Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number. For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.) c. translations.title: How Much is 10,000? PLC Activity
translations.explanation: How Much is 10,000? PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “From Hundredths to Hundred-thousands”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.NBT.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right. For example, recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: How Much is 10,000? PLC Activity. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 486 has 4 hundreds, 8 tens, and 6 ones, so 486 = 400 + 80 + 6. Adding 63 gives 486 + 63 = 549. Example 2: The number 867 has 8 hundreds, 6 tens, and 7 ones, so 867 = 800 + 60 + 7. Adding 38 gives 867 + 38 = 905.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 486 by place value. Step 2: decompose 63 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 549; estimate 486+about 63 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 867 by place value. Step 2: decompose 38 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 905; estimate 867+about 38 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: How Much is 10,000? PLC Activity. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: How Much is 10,000? PLC Activity. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

translations.title: Interpret Representations of Multiplicative Comparison PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Interpret Representations of Multiplicative Comparison PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Multiplicative Comparison and Measurement”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.OA.A.1, CCSS:4.OA.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations. Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.1 Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Interpret Representations of Multiplicative Comparison PLC Activity. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 7 equal groups with 7 objects in each group. The product is 7 × 7 = 49; therefore 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Example 2: Arrange 4 equal groups with 5 objects in each group. The product is 4 × 5 = 20; therefore 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 7 groups and 7 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 7 by 7 to get 49. Step 3: interpret 49 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Step 1: identify 4 groups and 5 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 4 by 5 to get 20. Step 3: interpret 20 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Interpret Representations of Multiplicative Comparison PLC Activity. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Interpret Representations of Multiplicative Comparison PLC Activity. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Ułóż 7 równych grup po 7 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 7 × 7 = 49, więc 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Przykład 2: Ułóż 4 równych grup po 5 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 4 × 5 = 20, więc 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozpoznaj 7 grup po 7 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 7 przez 7 i otrzymaj 49. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 49 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Krok 1: rozpoznaj 4 grup po 5 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 4 przez 5 i otrzymaj 20. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 20 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Mnożenie i dzielenie — Interpret Representations of Multiplicative Comparison PLC Activity. Nie zamieniaj bez sprawdzenia liczby grup z liczbą elementów w grupie. Resztę z dzielenia trzeba zinterpretować, a nie automatycznie pominąć. Gdy to możliwe, sprawdzaj dzielenie za pomocą mnożenia.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Mnożenie i dzielenie — Interpret Representations of Multiplicative Comparison PLC Activity. Wyraźnie modeluj równe grupy, łącz mnożenie z dzieleniem, licz dokładnie i interpretuj wynik w kontekście.

translations.title: Meters and Centimeters

translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 11×4=44. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(11+4)=30. translations.title: Multi-step Measurement Problems
translations.explanation: Multi-step Measurement Problems is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Multiplicative Comparison and Measurement”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.MD.A.2, CCSS:4.OA.A.2, CCSS:4.OA.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.1 Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole- number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding. 1See Glossary, Table 2. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Multi-step Measurement Problems. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 7 equal groups with 7 objects in each group. The product is 7 × 7 = 49; therefore 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Example 2: Arrange 8 equal groups with 8 objects in each group. The product is 8 × 8 = 64; therefore 64 ÷ 8 = 8.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 7 groups and 7 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 7 by 7 to get 49. Step 3: interpret 49 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Step 1: identify 8 groups and 8 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 8 by 8 to get 64. Step 3: interpret 64 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 64 ÷ 8 = 8.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Multi-step Measurement Problems. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Multi-step Measurement Problems. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

translations.title: Patterns that Grow PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Patterns that Grow PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Multiplying and Dividing Multi-digit Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.OA.C.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule “Add 3” and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Patterns that Grow PLC Activity. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 3 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 3 × 3 = 9; therefore 9 ÷ 3 = 3. Example 2: Arrange 7 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 7 × 3 = 21; therefore 21 ÷ 7 = 3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 3 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 3 by 3 to get 9. Step 3: interpret 9 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 9 ÷ 3 = 3. Step 1: identify 7 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 7 by 3 to get 21. Step 3: interpret 21 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 21 ÷ 7 = 3.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Patterns that Grow PLC Activity. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Patterns that Grow PLC Activity. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

Krok 1: rozpoznaj 7 grup po 3 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 7 przez 3 i otrzymaj 21. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 21 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 21 ÷ 7 = 3.

translations.explanation: Products Beyond 100 is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Multiplying and Dividing Multi-digit Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.NBT.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Products Beyond 100. A digit has a value determined by its position. Step 4: the sum is 375; estimate 318+about 57 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 499 by place value. Step 2: decompose 42 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 541; estimate 499+about 42 to confirm the magnitude.

translations.title: Situations Involving Area PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Situations Involving Area PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Multiplying and Dividing Multi-digit Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.MD.A.3, CCSS:4.NBT.B.6, CCSS:4.OA.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real world and mathematical problems. For example, find the width of a rectangular room given the area of the flooring and the length, by viewing the area formula as a multiplication equation with an unknown factor. Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models. Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole- number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding. 1See Glossary, Table 2. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Situations Involving Area PLC Activity. Choose a unit that matches the attribute, use equal-size units without gaps or overlaps, record the unit with the number, and interpret tables, line plots, clocks, money, area, volume, or angle measures according to the problem.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle measures 8 units by 5 units. Its area is 8 × 5 = 40 square units, while its perimeter is 2(8+5) = 26 units. Example 2: A rectangle measures 12 units by 7 units. Its area is 12 × 7 = 84 square units, while its perimeter is 2(12+7) = 38 units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 8×5=40. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(8+5)=26. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter. Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 12×7=84. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(12+7)=38. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Situations Involving Area PLC Activity. A number without its unit can be incomplete. Do not mix incompatible units before converting them. In graphs, read the scale and labels before drawing conclusions; in geometric measurement, distinguish length, area, angle, and volume.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Situations Involving Area PLC Activity. Identify what is measured, choose or convert units correctly, calculate or read the representation, and state the result with its unit and meaning.

translations.title: Division With and Without Remainders
translations.explanation: Division With and Without Remainders is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Multiplying and Dividing Multi-digit Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.NBT.B.6, CCSS:4.OA.A.3, CCSS:4.OA.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models. Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole- number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding. 1See Glossary, Table 2. Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1–100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1–100 is prime or composite. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Division With and Without Remainders. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 4 equal groups with 7 objects in each group. The product is 4 × 7 = 28; therefore 28 ÷ 4 = 7. Example 2: Arrange 7 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 7 × 3 = 21; therefore 21 ÷ 7 = 3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 4 groups and 7 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 4 by 7 to get 28. Step 3: interpret 28 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 28 ÷ 4 = 7. Step 1: identify 7 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 7 by 3 to get 21. Step 3: interpret 21 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 21 ÷ 7 = 3.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Division With and Without Remainders. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Division With and Without Remainders. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

translations.title: Problems About Perimeter and Area PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Problems About Perimeter and Area PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Multiplying and Dividing Multi-digit Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.MD.A.2, CCSS:4.MD.A.3, CCSS:4.OA.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale. Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real world and mathematical problems. For example, find the width of a rectangular room given the area of the flooring and the length, by viewing the area formula as a multiplication equation with an unknown factor. Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole- number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding. 1See Glossary, Table 2. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Problems About Perimeter and Area PLC Activity. Choose a unit that matches the attribute, use equal-size units without gaps or overlaps, record the unit with the number, and interpret tables, line plots, clocks, money, area, volume, or angle measures according to the problem.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle measures 12 units by 7 units. Its area is 12 × 7 = 84 square units, while its perimeter is 2(12+7) = 38 units. Example 2: A rectangle measures 12 units by 9 units. Its area is 12 × 9 = 108 square units, while its perimeter is 2(12+9) = 42 units.

translations.explanation: Estimation Exploration is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.OA.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole- number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Estimation Exploration. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 5 equal groups with 6 objects in each group. The product is 5 × 6 = 30; therefore 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Example 2: Arrange 8 equal groups with 8 objects in each group. The product is 8 × 8 = 64; therefore 64 ÷ 8 = 8.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 5 groups and 6 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 5 by 6 to get 30. Step 3: interpret 30 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Step 1: identify 8 groups and 8 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 8 by 8 to get 64. Step 3: interpret 64 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 64 ÷ 8 = 8.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Estimation Exploration. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Estimation Exploration. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Krok 1: rozpoznaj 8 grup po 8 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 8 przez 8 i otrzymaj 64. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 64 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 64 ÷ 8 = 8.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Mnożenie i dzielenie — Estimation Exploration. Nie zamieniaj bez sprawdzenia liczby grup z liczbą elementów w grupie. Resztę z dzielenia trzeba zinterpretować, a nie automatycznie pominąć. Gdy to możliwe, sprawdzaj dzielenie za pomocą mnożenia.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Mnożenie i dzielenie — Estimation Exploration. Wyraźnie modeluj równe grupy, łącz mnożenie z dzieleniem, licz dokładnie i interpretuj wynik w kontekście.

translations.title: Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.G.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 4 and 7 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 4 × 7 = 28 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 7 and 2 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 7 × 2 = 14 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 4 and 7. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 28. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 7 and 2. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 14. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Geometria — Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Geometria — Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity” należy do działu „Putting It All Together” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:4.G.A.1. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń opisuje, składa, rozkłada, porównuje i analizuje figury na podstawie ich cech definiujących, a nie wyłącznie wyglądu. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Geometria — Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity. Wnioski geometryczne powinny opierać się na takich własnościach jak boki, kąty, proste równoległe lub prostopadłe, symetria, współrzędne, przystawanie, podobieństwo albo równe części. Rysunek jest dowodem tylko wtedy, gdy znane lub zaznaczone własności uzasadniają wniosek.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Prostokąt o bokach 4 i 7 ma cztery kąty proste oraz równe boki przeciwległe. Jego pole to 4 × 7 = 28 jednostek kwadratowych. Przykład 2: Prostokąt o bokach 7 i 2 ma cztery kąty proste oraz równe boki przeciwległe. Jego pole to 7 × 2 = 14 jednostek kwadratowych.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozpoznaj cechy definiujące: cztery boki i cztery kąty proste. Krok 2: użyj długości 4 i 7. Krok 3: pomnóż i otrzymaj pole 28. Krok 4: zauważ, że obrót figury nie zmienia jej własności. Krok 1: rozpoznaj cechy definiujące: cztery boki i cztery kąty proste. Krok 2: użyj długości 7 i 2. Krok 3: pomnóż i otrzymaj pole 14. Krok 4: zauważ, że obrót figury nie zmienia jej własności.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Geometria — Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity. Nie klasyfikuj figury według obrotu, koloru lub wielkości, jeśli nie są to cechy definiujące. Nie odczytuj długości ani kąta wyłącznie z wyglądu rysunku; użyj podanych własności lub obliczeń.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Geometria — Which One Doesn’t Belong? PLC Activity. Nazwij istotne własności, poprawnie przedstaw figurę, wyciągnij wniosek z tych własności i sprawdź, czy pozostaje prawdziwy po zmianie obrotu lub skali rysunku.

translations.title: Number Talk
translations.explanation: Number Talk is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:4.NBT.A.1, CCSS:4.NF.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right. For example, recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division. Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number. a. Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b. For example, use a visual fraction model to represent 5/4 as the product 5 × (1/4), recording the conclusion by the equation 5/4 = 5 × (1/4). b. Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number. For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.) c. Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem. For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie? 3Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Number Talk. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 625 has 6 hundreds, 2 tens, and 5 ones, so 625 = 600 + 20 + 5. Adding 20 gives 625 + 20 = 645. Example 2: The number 466 has 4 hundreds, 6 tens, and 6 ones, so 466 = 400 + 60 + 6. Adding 31 gives 466 + 31 = 497.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 625 by place value. Step 2: decompose 20 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 645; estimate 625+about 20 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 466 by place value. Step 2: decompose 31 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 497; estimate 466+about 31 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Number Talk. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Number Talk. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

translations.title: Liczba Talk
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Liczba Talk” należy do działu „Putting It All Together” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:4.NBT.A.1, CCSS:4.NF.B.4. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń wykorzystuje strukturę systemu dziesiętnego do odczytywania, składania, rozkładania, porównywania, zaokrąglania i wykonywania działań na liczbach całkowitych lub dziesiętnych odpowiednio do poziomu. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Liczba Talk. Wartość cyfry zależy od jej pozycji. Przesunięcie o jedno miejsce w lewo mnoży wartość pozycyjną przez 10, a w prawo dzieli ją przez 10. Poprawne algorytmy zachowują wartości pozycyjne przez ustawianie tych samych rzędów pod sobą i właściwe przegrupowanie.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Liczba 625 ma 6 setek, 2 dziesiątek i 5 jedności, więc 625 = 600 + 20 + 5. Po dodaniu 20 otrzymujemy 625 + 20 = 645. Przykład 2: Liczba 466 ma 4 setek, 6 dziesiątek i 6 jedności, więc 466 = 400 + 60 + 6. Po dodaniu 31 otrzymujemy 466 + 31 = 497.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozłóż 625 według wartości pozycyjnych. Krok 2: w razie potrzeby rozłóż 20. Krok 3: połącz te same rzędy i przegrupuj dziesięć jednostek w jednostkę wyższego rzędu. Krok 4: wynik to 645; oszacuj, aby sprawdzić jego wielkość. Krok 1: rozłóż 466 według wartości pozycyjnych. Krok 2: w razie potrzeby rozłóż 31. Krok 3: połącz te same rzędy i przegrupuj dziesięć jednostek w jednostkę wyższego rzędu. Krok 4: wynik to 497; oszacuj, aby sprawdzić jego wielkość.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Liczba Talk. Nie porównuj liczb na podstawie jednej cyfry. W zapisie działań ustawiaj te same wartości pozycyjne pod sobą, szczególnie przy liczbach dziesiętnych. Szacuj wynik, aby wykrywać przesunięte cyfry i nierozsądne odpowiedzi.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Liczba Talk. Wykorzystaj wartość pozycyjną do przedstawienia liczby, wybierz skuteczną strategię działania lub porównania i sprawdź wielkość wyniku.
